title.en: The Grand Unity of the East: The First Hymn of the Nine Songs

region.en: The rite-ground of the Chu court (Hubei)

texts.period: Chu Ci, Jiu Ge, 4th-3rd c. BCE

source.work: Chu Ci, Jiu Ge: Dong Huang Tai Yi, the opening hymn of the grand rite

texts.license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: The first hymn of the Nine Songs names the highest: the Grand Unity of the East — the One beneath all the gods. The rite is all preparation and no narrative: a day set on an auspicious star, jade-stuffed bamboo, cinnamon wine, herbs of the altar laid in rows, the shamaness in her flowered robes singing softly, drums and strings rising — and the god, pleased, gives the blessing of harmony in return for the sincerity of the rite.
summary.zh: 吉日兮辰良，穆將愉兮上皇；撫長劍兮玉珥，璆鏘鳴兮琳瑯……五音紛兮繁會，君欣欣兮樂康——九歌之首，祭太一。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Chu Ci original. The Grand Unity became the supreme theological figure of Han state cult and, much later, the Jade Emperor's precursor.

passages.text: An auspicious day and a well-chosen hour: the rite makes ready to delight the Sovereign on High. The shamaness takes up the long sword with its jade pommel, the bells of her girdle ringing as she moves, and lays the altar with rows of herbs and meats in flower-strewn mats.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Chu Ci, Jiu Ge: Dong Huang Tai Yi (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: Cinnamon wine mixed with pepper-herbs is poured; the drum-sticks are raised, the slow beating begins, and the five notes mingle in their heap of sound. The god, well pleased, grants the blessing he keeps for the sincere — the Grand Unity honored, the year made whole.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Chu Ci, Jiu Ge: Dong Huang Tai Yi; not verbatim.

region.en: The sky-roads over the Chu lands (symbolic pin: cloud reaches)

texts.period: Chu Ci, Jiu Ge, 4th-3rd c. BCE

source.work: Chu Ci, Jiu Ge: Yunzhong Jun, the cloud-god's bath and passage

texts.license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: The Lord Within the Clouds bathes in the orchid soup, washes his hair in the fragrant steam, and passes along the sky in rainbow colors and dragon robes — the shamaness sings of his staying and going as of a lover who grants no tenure: he abides over Ji province with more than a mortal's power, then is gone beyond the clouds, and the heart follows him into the far light.
summary.zh: 浴蘭湯兮沐芳，華采衣兮若英；靈連蜷兮既留，爛昭昭兮未央……龍駕兮帝服，聊翱遊兮周章——雲中君之降與去。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Chu Ci original.

passages.text: The god bathes in the soup of orchid and washes his hair in the fragrant steam, robed in the flower's own colors; he lingers, glowing, in the shrine of the rite, brighter than the ends of things. He rides a dragon's carriage in the dress of an emperor, wheels and circles through the nine provinces; his light abides there, and the singer's heart goes after him into the dark — for the cloud-lord, like all the lords of the Nine Songs, grants a visit and not a residence.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Chu Ci, Jiu Ge: Yunzhong Jun (compiler's rendering); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Chu Ci, Jiu Ge: Yunzhong Jun; not verbatim.

title.en: The River Lord, in the Hall of Shellfish and the Palace of Fish

region.en: The Nine-River ford and the River Lord's water-halls (Yellow River)

texts.period: Chu Ci, Jiu Ge, 4th-3rd c. BCE

source.work: Chu Ci, Jiu Ge: He Bo, the river-god's hall of shells and the white turtle's dance

texts.license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: The River Lord's hymn is a tour of the water-world: he plays with the nine rivers, breaks the ice of the Kunlun ford, rides his white turtle to a hall of shells and a palace of fish, follows the girl into the far isles, and at the ford they part — his hall of glories lies westward, and the singer watches the wave-face of the water carry him away.
summary.zh: 與女遊兮九河，衝風起兮橫波；乘水車兮荷蓋，駕兩龍兮驂螭……魚鱗屋兮龍堂，紫貝闕兮朱宮——河伯之遊。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Chu Ci original.

passages.text: The River Lord and his guest go up the nine rivers together, wind rising athwart the waves; he drives a water-carriage roofed with lotus, drawn by two dragons harnessed with the sea-horse team. He climbs the Kunlun ford and watches the world's end, his heart flying like sunlight on the water; he lodges in a house walled with fish-scales, in a hall of dragon-beams, behind gates of purple shell and vermilion palaces — the water-world as the shamaness tours it, god-guided.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Chu Ci, Jiu Ge: He Bo (compiler's rendering); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Chu Ci, Jiu Ge: He Bo; not verbatim.

passages.text: They wander to the isle of the far islets, where the waters wheel; and the hymn ends at the ford with the farewell: his hall of glories lies toward the sunset, and the fish-neighbor greets him as he goes — the river-god's day of hospitality, closed at the crossing.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Chu Ci, Jiu Ge: He Bo; not verbatim.

title.en: The Great Summons: The Feast Laid for a Returning Soul

region.en: The Chu mourning-grounds and the halls of Ying

texts.period: Chu Ci, Dazhao (The Great Summons), 3rd c. BCE

source.work: Chu Ci, Dazhao (The Great Summons): the four quarters' perils named again, and the catalog of feasts for the soul's return

texts.license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: The Great Summons, companion-piece to the Summons of the Soul, calls the dead home by naming the perils of the four quarters and the six directions — and then lays out the feast of the Chu court in verse: wines, roasts, soups, fruits, music and dancers, a catalog of everything a household was, set out as the reason to return.
summary.zh: 魂乎歸來！四方上下皆不可託；楚廷之宴——酒漿、炙雁、龜羹、蜜餌、鐘鼓樂舞——以宴致魂。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Chu Ci original. Companion to chinese-chuci-zhaohun.

passages.text: The Great Summons calls the soul home by the same four-quarters litany as its companion piece: do not go east, or south, or west, or north, or up, or down — each direction named with its devourers, its ice, its sand, its dark capital — and home named with its gate of bright walls.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Chu Ci, Dazhao (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then the feast: the wines of the frost and the spring, the roast swan and the fat goose, the turtle-soup and the lamb, the honey-baits and the spiced duck, the music of the bells and the pipes, the dancers of the court — a catalog in verse of everything a household was, laid out as the reason to return. The soul is argued with by luxury rather than by fear, and the rite works both arguments at once.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Chu Ci, Dazhao, the feast catalog; not verbatim.

title.en: The Cowherd and the Weaver Girl: Two Stars and One Bridge of Birds

region.en: The Milky Way's two banks and the river of the sky (symbolic pin: the sky itself)

texts.period: Folk cycle; oldest layer in Shi Jing, Xiao Ya: Da Dong (c. 8th-6th c. BCE); festival charter in Jingchu Suishiji, 6th c. CE

source.work: The Cowherd-Weaver cycle: the Ox Star and the Weaver Star, the magpie bridge of the seventh night, and the river of stars between them

texts.license: Public domain (folk tradition; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: The Weaver Girl of the sky wove the clouds at her loom and loved the Cowherd across the river of stars; the marriage pleased no one in heaven — she stopped weaving, and the separation was decreed: one night a year, the seventh of the seventh month, when all the magpies of the world fly up to make a bridge of their own bodies across the star-river and the two meet on the birds' backs in the dark. The rest of the year the river runs between them, and rain on that night is said to be their tears.
summary.zh: 織女為天帝之女，年年機杼，織雲錦天衣；牛郎織女隔天河相望——七月初七，鵲橋相會，一年一度；「迢迢牽牛星，皎皎河漢女」——乞巧節由此而立。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the folk cycle. Tagging caveat: 'sun-capture' marks the sky-star pair motif, interpretive. The festival (Qixi) is living heritage; the record is archival.

passages.text: In the sky-river's two banks two stars keep their places: the Weaver on the east, the Cowherd with his ox on the west. She wove the cloud-robes of heaven, he herded the sky's cattle, and the two loved across the water of stars.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Cowherd-Weaver folk cycle (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: The marriage so pleased neither court nor loom — the clouds went unwoven while she was happy — that a decree set the river between them forever, with one night of reunion each year. On the seventh night of the seventh month the magpies of the whole world fly up and spread themselves wing to wing as a bridge, and the Weaver walks across the birds to the Cowherd's side of the sky.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the folk cycle with the Qixi charter; not verbatim.

passages.text: The girls of China lay out needles in the water that night to beg a thread of her skill — the feast of Begging for Skill — and if rain falls on the bridge of birds it is called the tears the couple cannot shed at any other time of the sky's year.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Qixi festival customs; not verbatim.

title.en: Meng Jiangnü Weeps Down the Great Wall

region.en: The Great Wall works at Shanhaiguan (pin: Hebei coast)

texts.period: Folk cycle; earliest layer in Zuo Zhuan, Xiang 23 (c. 4th c. BCE text); Tang Dunhuang bianwen recension; Ming shrines

source.work: The Meng Jiangnü cycle: the girl of the gourd-vine, the conscripted husband, and the weeping that cracked the wall

texts.license: Public domain (folk tradition; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Two neighboring households raised a girl born from a gourd-vine that grew across both their walls; she married the young man Fan Xiliang, who was seized three days after the wedding for the Great Wall's works. She sewed winter clothes through the autumn and walked the whole wall north to find him — and found that he was dead, built into the wall's fill. Her weeping went on for days until the wall cracked for three hundred li and showed the bones; her blood marked her husband's among the nameless, and the First Emperor, arriving to punish the weeper, offered her what no one had offered before — and she chose the sea.
summary.zh: 孟姜女為兩家共植瓜藤所生，嫁范喜良；婚後三日夫被抓修長城；千里送寒衣，哭崩長城三百里，滴血認夫骨；始皇欲納之，姜女投海——貞女祠由此而立。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the folk cycle. The tale is a protest-legend against corvée labor; its layers (Zuo Zhuan's chaste widow, Tang bianwen, Ming folk drama) show a millennium of retelling.

passages.text: A gourd-vine planted by one household climbed the wall and fruited in the yard of the other, and from the gourd came a girl both families claimed; they raised her together as Meng Jiangnü, the child of the shared vine.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Meng Jiangnü folk cycle (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: She had been married three days when the conscription took her husband Fan to the Great Wall's works; through the autumn she sewed winter clothes and walked the whole northern line to bring them to him — and learned at the works that he had died in the wall's own fill, one body among thousands.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the folk cycle; not verbatim.

passages.text: She sat against the wall and wept until it cracked open for three hundred li, and the bones lay bare; her blood, dropped on the nameless heap, found and marked her husband's. The First Emperor came himself to punish the weeper and offered instead to marry her; she asked for a state funeral for her husband, rode out to the sea at the rite's end, and stepped off the cliff into the water rather than be the emperor's bride.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the folk cycle, the emperor and the sea; not verbatim.

title.en: Liang Shanbo and Zhu Yingtai: The Butterfly Tomb

region.en: Hangzhou and Ningbo, the school and the tomb (Zhejiang)

texts.period: Folk cycle; earliest Tang citations; full flowering in Song-Ming drama and storyteller books

source.work: The Liang-Zhu cycle: the girl disguised as a boy, the school of Hangzhou, the tomb that opened for the coffin

texts.license: Public domain (folk tradition; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Zhu Yingtai dressed as a boy to study at the Hangzhou academy, and three years as deskmate taught Liang Shanbo everything about her but the one thing; she went home betrothed to another, and he died of the discovery. Her wedding procession stopped at his grave on the way; she wept, the tomb cracked open, and she stepped in — the grave closed on the two of them, and out of it rose two butterflies that flew together and did not part: the folk corpus's great love-death, and the reason Chinese butterfly pairs mean marriage.
summary.zh: 祝英臺女扮男裝入杭州求學，與梁山伯同窗三年；英臺許配馬家，山伯鬱鬱而終；英臺出嫁路經墓前，哭而墓裂，入墓合葬——化為雙蝶雙飛。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the folk cycle.

passages.text: Zhu Yingtai cut her hair, bound her chest, and enrolled at the Hangzhou academy as a boy, with a servant carrying her books; three years at the same desk taught Liang Shanbo her mind, her humor, her hand at the lute — everything about her but that she was a girl.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Liang-Zhu folk cycle (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: She went home and left him hints he was too honest to read — the duck-and-mandarin pair, the well's two reflections — and was betrothed in her absence to the son of a rich house. He came to visit too late, understood, and died of it within the season.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the folk cycle; not verbatim.

passages.text: Her wedding procession passed his grave on the road to the other bridegroom's house, and she stopped it, wept, and prayed at the stone; the tomb split, she stepped in, the earth closed on the two of them — and two butterflies rose from the mound and flew together, wing for wing, out of the mourning crowd's sight.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the folk cycle, the butterfly ending; not verbatim.

title.en: The Eight Immortals Cross the Sea, Each by His Own Art

region.en: The eastern sea, between Penglai and the mainland (Shandong coast)

texts.period: Dongyou Ji (Journey to the East) by Wu Yuantai, Ming, c. 1562; cult much older

source.work: Dongyou Ji, juan on the sea-crossing: the eight immortals' crossing of the eastern sea, each riding his own treasure

texts.license: Public domain (Ming novel; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Feasting at the pebble-beach after the Peach Banquet, the Eight Immortals refused the cloud-road home and crossed the sea instead, each riding his own treasure thrown on the waves: Zhongli Quan his fan, Lü Dongbin his sword, the girl He Xiangu her lotus flower, Iron-Crutch Li his crutch, Lan Caihe his flower-basket, Zhang Guolao his paper mule, Han Xiangzi his flute, and Royal Uncle Cao his jade tablets. The Dragon King's son stole He Xiangu, and the war that followed set the sea boiling — the eight of them against the four seas' hosts, ending with the immortals on top and a new temple on Penglai.
summary.zh: 八仙過東海，各顯神通：鍾離權扇、呂洞賓劍、何仙姑蓮花、鐵拐李拐、藍采和花籃、張果老紙驢、韓湘子笛、曹國舅玉板；龍王太子劫何仙姑，八仙大鬧龍宮——各憑本事。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Ming novel.

passages.text: Returning from the Peach Banquet over the eastern sea, the Eight Immortals refused the cloud-road Lü Dongbin offered and crossed on the water instead — each setting his own treasure on the waves and riding it: the fan, the sword, the lotus, the crutch, the flower-basket, the paper mule, the flute, the jade tablets of office.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dongyou Ji, sea-crossing chapter (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: The show drew the Dragon King's son, who dragged the girl-immortal He Xiangu down to the sea-palace; the seven came for her with fire and frost and mountain-moving, and the four seas' hosts could not hold them — the immortals left with their own, the dragon-court fined, and the crossing entered the saying-books as the Chinese standard for eight people, eight methods, one shore.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dongyou Ji; not verbatim.

title.en: Wu Gang Chops the Cassia That Heals Itself

region.en: The moon's cassia tree (symbolic pin: the moon)

texts.period: Youyang Zazu by Duan Chengshi, c. 860 CE, Tianchi section

source.work: Youyang Zazu, Tianchi: Wu Gang of Hexi, the cassia tree of the moon, and the blows that never finish

texts.license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: In the moon stands a cassia tree five hundred zhang tall, under which a man named Wu Gang, exiled from the Hexi country for his faults in seeking the Way, chops at the trunk forever: the tree closes every wound as the axe lifts, ten thousand blows and none of them the last. The moon's shadow on clear nights is the tree; the man under it, said the Tang book, is the reason the tree is always whole and always being cut.
summary.zh: 月桂高五百丈，下有一人常斫之，樹創隨合；人姓吳名剛，西河人，學仙有過，謫令伐樹——萬世之斧與一樹之癒。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Youyang Zazu text.

passages.text: In the moon stands a cassia tree five hundred zhang tall, and under it a man named Wu Gang, of the Hexi country, chops at the trunk with an axe; the wound in the wood closes before the axe can be lifted, so that every blow is the first and none of them the last.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Youyang Zazu, Tianchi section, Wu Gang entry (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: He was sent there, says the Tang book, for faults in his seeking of the Way — a student exiled to an unfinishable labor in the brightest place in the sky. The moon's shadowed face on a clear night is the tree; the reason it is always whole and always being cut stands below it, swinging.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Youyang Zazu; not verbatim.
